name: Arcade Learning Environment
ability_definition: The ability to time your movements or the movement of a piece of equipment in anticipation of changes in the speed and/or direction of a moving object or scene.

task_realism.reasoning: A subset of games (Pong, Breakout, Tennis, Boxing, some shooters) does require anticipating the trajectory and speed changes of moving objects and timing an intercept or hit. This is the core of Rate Control. However, these are stylized 2D arcade dynamics with simple, often deterministic physics. They are far removed from workplace cases such as operating cranes or forklifts, driving, catching or striking objects in sports, or tracking targets with equipment. Many of the 57 games (Montezuma's Revenge, Pitfall, Venture) are mainly about exploration or puzzles, not timing.

evaluation_conditions.reasoning: The emulator runs in discrete steps with frame-skipping, so the agent faces no true real-time latency constraint and can use huge amounts of training experience on the exact test environments. Sticky actions add a little stochasticity, but the input distribution is fixed, has low variability, and is memorizable. There is no sensorimotor delay, no physical actuator noise, no consequence for failure, and no shift to new object speeds or paths. Real-world timing tasks involve all of these.

construct_coverage.reasoning: The headline Atari-57 metric (mean HNS) mixes timing-heavy games with games dominated by exploration, credit assignment and long-horizon planning. It is also uncapped and driven by outlier games. Nothing in the metric isolates timing accuracy or interception success, and object speed and path are not systematically varied. Rate Control therefore contributes only a small and uncontrolled share of the aggregate score.

format_match.reasoning: The input is low-resolution game pixels and the output is a discrete joystick or button action chosen from up to 18 options. Real work involves continuous control of limbs or equipment in 3D scenes, with depth perception and proprioceptive feedback. The visual-scene-to-action loop has some structural similarity, but the artifacts are game-like, not work-like.

transferability_reasoning: ALE contains some games that genuinely exercise anticipatory timing against moving objects, but its aggregate score mostly reflects exploration and credit assignment across diverse games. It is measured under step-based, heavily trained, low-variability conditions with discrete pixel-game controls. Performance on it transfers only weakly and indirectly to real-world Rate Control, which fits its role as a demoted fallback for the better-aligned Robot Air Hockey Challenge.

2021.metric: mean human-normalized score across 57 Atari games (%)
2021.human_reference: General adult population performing real-time visuomotor timing tasks. Operationalized by the ALE human baseline: a professional game tester after about 2 hours of practice per game, roughly a competent, somewhat-above-median player.

2025.metric: percent, mean human-normalized score (HNS) across the 57 Atari games
2025.human_reference: General adult workforce performing real-time timing and control tasks such as operators and drivers. The ALE human baseline (a professional game tester with brief practice) serves as a proxy for a typical-to-somewhat-above-typical human.
